strengths: The paper addresses a concrete and practically important problem: using LLMs to automate HLS-C generation, debugging, and pragma-based optimization, where tool feedback and domain constraints are genuinely difficult for general code models.
The proposed workflow is reasonably well motivated, separating generation, tuning, error analysis, repair, and verification agents rather than relying on a single prompt-only model.

The paper reports nontrivial empirical results, including 612 debugging cases over 33 HLS designs and ablations suggesting that analysis, DPO, and iterative multi-model feedback each improve repair pass rate.
The VODA/BugRAG idea of constructing HLS-specific error slices and synthetic buggy-code examples is a plausible contribution for domain adaptation of code LMs.
weaknesses: The paper is only marginally aligned with ACL/NLP: the main contribution is an EDA/HLS automation system, and the linguistic/modeling novelty is limited mostly to fine-tuning and multi-agent prompting with domain-specific data.

Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript does not provide enough detail on data splits, exact prompts, generated datasets, source code, evaluation scripts, model checkpoints, API settings for GPT-4o/Claude, or whether the manually crafted designs and bug cases will be released.

The debugging evaluation may substantially overestimate generalization because the test errors appear closely tied to the same taxonomy and synthetic bug-injection process used to build the training data; leakage controls are asserted but not convincingly specified.
The optimization evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims: HLSTuner is tested on only five PolyBench kernels, yet the paper claims broad design-space navigation and SOTA speedups.

Comparisons to DSL-based and learning-based HLS methods are not sufficiently controlled. It is unclear whether baselines receive equivalent tuning budgets, target constraints, hardware settings, source transformations, and optimization objectives.

The energy-efficiency metric is a proxy introduced by the authors, but key choices such as the sensitivity coefficient and rationale for the functional form are underexplained; this weakens claims based on Figure 11.

Several central implementation details remain underspecified, including how BugRAG retrieval is performed, how new error types are validated, how the scoring agent is calibrated, how failed repair attempts are counted, and how semantic equivalence is checked beyond passing available tests.

The paper sometimes overstates conclusions relative to evidence, e.g. describing five kernels as sufficient to show strong generalization potential and presenting headline speedups without enough uncertainty analysis or per-baseline methodological detail.

Clarity is uneven: figures contain duplicated or crowded content, some labels are hard to interpret from the text extraction, and there are typos/terminology issues such as 'Abaltion' and inconsistent naming of Llama3/Llama3.1.

strengths: The paper targets a concrete and practically important problem: automating HLS code repair and directive optimization, where tool feedback provides an objective verification signal.

The proposed workflow combines several sensible ingredients: HLS-tool-in-the-loop validation, error-type retrieval, supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, and iterative repair. The reported repair pass rate and speedups, if reproducible, would be useful to the HLS/EDA community.
The evaluation includes some ablations for HLSFixer and compares against general LLMs and several HLS optimization baselines, which is directionally appropriate.
weaknesses: The paper is weakly aligned with ACL/CL/NLP. The central contribution is an EDA/HLS automation system, with little methodological novelty for language modeling, code intelligence, or NLP beyond applying existing LLM fine-tuning and multi-agent prompting machinery.

The methodology is underspecified. The paper does not provide enough detail about prompts, agent orchestration, BugRAG construction, error taxonomy, data generation filters, train/test splitting, decoding settings, LoRA configuration, DPO setup, or baseline prompting to reproduce the main results.

The evidence for the strongest claims is thin. HLSTuner is evaluated on only five PolyBench kernels, yet the paper makes broad claims about generalization and practical HLS optimization. This is too small a benchmark for the claimed scope.

There is substantial risk of data leakage or overly easy synthetic evaluation. The debugging dataset is generated through controlled bug insertion from known error slices, and the test cases appear closely related to the same error taxonomy and sources. The paper does not convincingly show that the model handles naturally occurring, unseen HLS failures.

Baseline comparisons are not sufficiently rigorous. General LLMs, RAG-based methods, DSL-based methods, and learning-based DSE systems solve somewhat different tasks under unclear attempt budgets and constraints. The paper does not clearly normalize compute budget, search budget, resource constraints, or implementation effort.

The optimization metrics are not well justified. The proposed energy-efficiency proxy is ad hoc, and the paper does not provide enough raw latency/resource tables for all systems to verify the plotted speedups or understand trade-offs.

The system relies on closed or large external models in several agents while also claiming reproducible fine-tuned components. The exact models used in LLM groups, scoring agents, and generation agents are unclear, which further weakens reproducibility.

Ablations are incomplete. The paper does not isolate the effect of VODA versus ordinary synthetic bug generation, BugRAG retrieval versus no retrieval, fine-tuning versus prompting under matched budgets, or iterative repair versus increased sampling.

Clarity and presentation are uneven. Several figures are crowded and difficult to parse, terminology is sometimes imprecise, and some claims are overstated relative to the experiments, such as asserting sufficient generalization from five kernels.

Overall, the submission does not currently support a sound, reproducible ACL contribution. A revised version would need a clearer NLP/code-modeling contribution, stronger experimental controls, public artifacts or detailed reproducibility materials, and a much broader and cleaner evaluation.

strengths: The paper addresses a concrete and practically important bottleneck: making HLS design more accessible by automating HLS-C repair and directive optimization with LLM-based agents. The motivation is clear, and the system targets failures that are specific to HLS rather than generic code generation errors.

The proposed workflow is reasonably complete: VODA constructs verification-oriented repair data, HLSFixer separates diagnosis from modification and validates fixes with HLS tools, and HLSTuner uses QoR feedback for optimization. This is more convincing than a purely prompt-based pipeline.

The empirical results are promising. HLSFixer is evaluated on 612 cases from 33 designs and 34 error types, with an 82.7% reported pass rate and useful ablations showing gains from analysis, DPO, and multi-agent iteration. The optimization results also show substantial speedups over general LLMs, RAG-based methods, and several HLS baselines on the reported kernels.

The paper provides useful implementation-level detail about training data sizes, model family, LoRA training, hardware, optimizer, learning rates, and evaluation platform, which helps make the contribution more concrete.

The contribution is potentially relevant to NLP/CL as an applied code-generation and domain adaptation study: it shows how LLMs can be aligned to a specialized programming/debugging domain through synthetic verification data and structured reasoning supervision.
weaknesses: The relevance to ACL is somewhat indirect. The main contribution is in HLS/EDA automation rather than language modeling, linguistic analysis, or broadly reusable NLP methodology. The paper would be stronger for ACL if it more clearly abstracted lessons about LLM adaptation, code repair, agent design, or verification-grounded data generation beyond this hardware domain.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper does not clearly state whether the datasets, prompts, BugRAG entries, trained adapters, code, train/test splits, generated kernels, and evaluation scripts will be released. Since the results depend on Vitis HLS, proprietary/commercial LLMs, generated CoT data, and several multi-agent decisions, independent reproduction may be difficult.

The optimization evaluation is narrow: HLSTuner is tested on only five PolyBench kernels. The paper claims strong generalization potential, but the evidence is limited for such a broad claim, especially given that HLS optimization behavior can vary substantially across applications, dataflow patterns, memory structures, and target devices.

Some comparisons need more detail to be fully convincing. It is not always clear whether baselines receive equal budgets, feedback loops, debugging assistance, or numbers of attempts. The comparisons against DSL-based and learning-based HLS methods may also be sensitive to implementation choices, target constraints, and whether source-level transformations are comparable to pragma insertion.

The methodology for synthetic bug generation and verification-oriented augmentation could introduce distributional artifacts. The paper says test cases are excluded from training, but it does not sufficiently analyze possible overlap in error templates, kernel families, generated bug patterns, or golden fixes between training and evaluation.

Several metrics and claims need tighter justification. The energy-efficiency metric is a proxy with design choices such as the latency activation and resource penalty that are not fully motivated or sensitivity-tested. Claims such as achieving reliable design optimization and maintaining expressivity are broader than what the experiments directly establish.

Presentation quality is uneven. Several figures are visually crowded or duplicated in extraction, some terminology is imprecise, and there are minor typos. More tables with exact numeric results would help readers verify the plotted improvements and understand variance across benchmarks.

strengths: The paper targets a concrete and practically important problem: using LLMs to generate, debug, and optimize HLS-C designs under synthesizability and QoR constraints. The framing of separate debugging and directive-tuning agents is sensible for this domain.
The work provides a reasonably complete system design, including HLSFixer, HLSTuner, BugRAG, VODA, tool-feedback parsing, fine-tuning, DPO, and iterative verification through CSIM/CSYN/COSIM.

The reported empirical gains are large: HLSFixer improves debugging pass rates over strong general-purpose LLMs and RAG baselines, and HLSTuner reports substantial latency speedups under resource constraints. The paper includes ablations and matched RAG baselines, which strengthen the case that retrieval alone is insufficient.

The evaluation uses actual HLS toolchain checks rather than only textual/code similarity metrics, and it reports relevant hardware metrics such as latency, DSP/FF/LUT utilization, and some post-implementation timing/power validation.
weaknesses: The paper is only partially aligned with ACL/NLP: much of the contribution is a domain-specific CAD/HLS automation system, and the NLP contribution beyond applying/fine-tuning LLM agents is not clearly separated from engineering integration.

Reproducibility is a major concern. The paper does not clearly commit to releasing the generated datasets, BugRAG entries, trained models, prompts in machine-usable form, scripts, or full benchmark/testbench setup. Several components depend on proprietary or API models, making exact reproduction difficult.

The train/test leakage analysis is weak. Rouge-L against aggregated training text is not a convincing leakage test for code/HLS tasks, especially when many examples are synthetic transformations of a small number of base designs and when teacher-generated rationales are produced from paired buggy/correct code.

The debugging evaluation may be overly favorable: many test cases are created by automated error injection and only retained when the HLS tool explicitly reports the injected error type, which may simplify diagnosis relative to natural, compound, or ambiguous HLS failures.

Baseline comparability is not fully convincing. Some comparisons use reported numbers from prior work with different pass-rate definitions or attempt budgets; other baselines are reproduced with limited details. The optimization comparisons also mix LLM, RAG, DSL, and DSE methods whose inputs, human effort, and search budgets are not always normalized.

The central mechanism claims around “QoR-aware reasoning” and “causal” understanding are stronger than the evidence supports. The model is trained on teacher explanations of verified before/after QoR pairs, but the paper does not rigorously show that the model has learned causal directive semantics rather than benchmark-specific heuristics.

The system is complex, with many agents and fallback paths, but the contribution of each component is not always isolated. The multi-LLM judge/fallback setup especially raises cost, reproducibility, and attribution questions.

The scope is limited to a small set of directives and primarily one FPGA platform, while claims about agile hardware development and general HLS optimization are broader than the demonstrated evidence.

strengths: The paper targets a real and practically important bottleneck in LLM-assisted high-level synthesis: synthesizability-aware code generation, debugging from tool feedback, and directive tuning under resource constraints.

The system is evaluated with HLS-tool validation rather than only textual/code-similarity metrics. Requiring CSIM, CSYN, and COSIM, plus limited post-implementation checks, is a meaningful strength for this domain.

The paper provides a fairly complete system description, including separate generation, debugging, data augmentation, and optimization components, and includes prompts, training settings, ablations, RAG baselines, and supplementary per-error/per-kernel analyses.

The reported empirical gains are large across debugging pass rates and directive optimization speedups, suggesting that domain-specific supervision and feedback-grounded repair may be useful for HLS workflows if validated more rigorously.
weaknesses: The paper is only weakly situated as an ACL/NLP contribution. The main novelty appears to be a hardware-design automation pipeline and dataset engineering for HLS rather than a generalizable NLP/modeling contribution. Its relevance to computational linguistics is therefore limited and needs much clearer framing.

The evaluation has serious soundness concerns. Training data, chain-of-thought rationales, bug injection, and some benchmark construction are all generated by DeepSeek-V3.2 or other LLM agents, and the paper does not provide enough evidence that the resulting test cases represent natural HLS errors rather than artifacts of the injection pipeline.

The train/test separation evidence is inadequate. Rouge-L against an aggregated training set is not a convincing leakage or memorization analysis for code/HLS designs, especially when train and test are drawn from small families of standard kernels and synthetically mutated errors.

The debugging benchmark is biased toward cases where the HLS tool explicitly reports the injected error type. Filtering test cases this way may exclude harder ambiguous failures and overestimate real-world robustness.

Baseline comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. Some baselines use reported numbers from prior work, RALAD is reproduced with GPT-5.1, different models are used for different roles, and the multi-agent system receives substantially more tool feedback/search/debugging machinery than single-model baselines. This makes the headline improvements difficult to attribute.

The optimization evaluation is hard to interpret: failed or invalid attempts are penalized in ways that may affect geometric means, the search budgets and prompt/tool interactions are not fully matched, and the paper does not clearly separate benefits from fine-tuning, iterative feedback, model size, and allowed number of synthesis trials.

Reproducibility is poor. I found no code, model, dataset, benchmark split, generated test cases, or scripts for running Vitis experiments. Given the dependence on proprietary tools, specific hardware, API models, and generated artifacts, the provided description is not enough to reproduce the main claims.

Several central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. Claims about causal QoR reasoning, generalization to unseen HLS designs, and avoidance of data contamination are asserted but not demonstrated with sufficiently independent benchmarks or human/expert validation.

The paper’s presentation contains duplicated figure content, dense and sometimes confusing system diagrams, and terminology such as many numbered LLM agents that makes the method harder to audit. Important experimental details are deferred or described qualitatively rather than operationally.

strengths: The paper addresses a concrete and important bottleneck in LLM-assisted HLS design, combining generation, directive tuning, tool-feedback debugging, and verification into a coherent end-to-end system.

The empirical results are strong across several axes: HLS-C generation pass rates, HLS-specific debugging pass@1, and directive-level optimization speedups. The inclusion of CSIM, CSYN, COSIM, resource constraints, and some post-implementation checks makes the evidence more convincing than purely text-level code-generation metrics.

The decomposition into HLSTuner, HLSFixer, and VODA is well motivated. In particular, the reasoning-to-instruction debugging setup and tool-feedback loop are plausible mechanisms for improving HLS-specific error repair.

The paper includes useful ablations and matched RAG baselines, showing that retrieval alone does not explain the gains. The appendix provides nontrivial implementation detail on training settings, prompts, datasets, metrics, and supported directives.

The work is likely useful to the LLM-for-code and design-automation communities, and it demonstrates a practical way to ground LLM agents in compiler/synthesis feedback rather than relying on free-form generation alone.
weaknesses: The contribution to core computational linguistics/NLP is somewhat indirect. The paper is primarily an applied LLM-agent system for HLS/CAD, with limited new modeling or language-understanding methodology beyond domain-specific fine-tuning, prompting, retrieval, and multi-agent orchestration.

Reproducibility is only partial. The system depends on proprietary or future-named API models, Vitis HLS tooling, generated datasets, and fine-tuned weights; it is unclear whether the data, code, prompts, trained models, and exact evaluation harness will be released in a form that enables independent replication.

The data construction and evaluation raise possible leakage and distribution concerns. Training and evaluation are both built around injected or generated HLS errors from overlapping source ecosystems, and the reported Rouge-L train-test similarity is a weak safeguard against semantic or structural overlap.

Baseline comparisons are not uniformly controlled. Some comparisons use reported numbers from prior work, some use reproduced RAG variants with different model backends and search budgets, and the optimization comparisons may differ in available resource budgets, number of trials, and degree of manual/domain-specific setup.

The debugging benchmark is heavily synthetic, based on injected errors and retained cases where the tool explicitly reports the injected error type. This may overestimate performance on naturally occurring, compound, ambiguous, or poorly localized HLS failures.

The optimization results are impressive but need more careful interpretation: HLSTuner can exploit up to an 80% resource budget, while some DSL or default baselines use far fewer resources. The speedup/resource trade-off is not always presented as a Pareto comparison.

The paper would benefit from clearer failure analysis and uncertainty estimates. Results are mostly point estimates, and it is hard to assess variance across prompts, random seeds, API model nondeterminism, and synthesis-tool instability.
